sentences.text: Devincenzia was a robust, bulky bird adapted for ambush hunting, making it larger and more massive than its relatives Phorusrhacos and Titanis.
This carnivorous animal may have also functioned as a scavenger.
The largest possible specimen could have reached 2 meters in height and weighed between 200 and 500 kilograms.
Large expansions on the lacrimal bone likely protected the eyes from the sun, suggesting keen vision in open, sunlit areas rather than shaded forests.
The genus was described by Lucas Kraglievich in 1932, following the initial description of fossils in 1931.
The first specimens were found in the Ituzaingó Formation in southern Argentina, a geological layer dating to the Late Miocene, a period of high biodiversity in South America.
These initial fossils were cataloged at the MACN under the numbers MACN PV 6554 and MACN PV 6681.
A separate Uruguayan specimen likely originates from the Arroyo Roman, dating to the Miocene or Oligocene.
Kraglievich originally placed Devincenzia in its own family, Devincenziidae, within the order Stereornithes, describing it as the sole member of this distinct group.
Recent studies consider Psilopteridae and Devincenziidae synonymous with Phorusrhacidae, though Brodkorb corrected the family name spelling from Phororhacidae to Phorusrhacidae in 1967.
A phorusrhacine tibiotarsus from the Early Pleistocene Raigón Formation of southern Uruguay was described in 1999.
Phorusrhacids dispersed into North America during the Great American Biotic Interchange approximately 3 million years ago.
A phorusrhacine from the La Venta Formation of Colombia is larger than the D. pozzi tibiotarsus.
Whether Onactornis and Devincenzia are synonyms remains a subject of debate.
The discovery of Kelenken challenged the traditional view that larger phorusrhacids were less agile and adapted for running.
Assignments of remains from Africa, Europe, and the Paleocene of Brazil to Phorusrhacidae or as related to seriemas remain controversial.
Agnolín's stance on Phorusrhacinae composition was backed by a phylogenetic analysis finding Kelenken and Devincenzia as sister taxa.
Researchers suggested future studies should examine if phorusrhacids used beaks and claws against well-armored mammals like armadillos and glyptodonts.
